result: The authors developed OT-TP-LSM, an open-top two-photon light sheet microscopy system for intraoperative 3D pathology. The system uses a scanned Bessel beam to generate an extended depth of field excitation light sheet, achieves imaging at 400 fps, and collects both fluorescence and SHG signals simultaneously through dual sCMOS cameras.
evaluation: Claims C3-C6, C31-C42, C44-C45, and C145-C147 provide comprehensive technical specifications and design details of the OT-TP-LSM system. The system architecture, optical components, beam generation method, and imaging parameters are clearly described with specific measurements. The open-top configuration with all components below the sample holder is well-documented.

result: The OT-TP-LSM system was characterized using fluorescent microspheres, achieving an image throughput of 0.24 mm²/s at 400 fps with 1 μm step size, and a measured resolution of 0.9 μm in all dimensions. The lateral resolution in the Y-Z' plane was approximately 128% of theoretical due to spherical aberration but was sufficient for detecting cellular features.
evaluation: Claims C46-C49 describe the characterization methodology and measured performance metrics. The use of fluorescent microspheres in RI-matched agarose gel is appropriate for system characterization. The measured resolution and throughput values are specific and quantitative. The acknowledgment of spherical aberration and its impact on resolution demonstrates rigorous characterization.

result: OT-TP-LSM achieved an imaging depth of approximately 64 μm from the surface in human skin specimens, which was approximately three times greater than conventional one-photon LSM (20 μm). While sufficient for visualizing 3D cell structures in skin, the imaging depth was relatively low compared to conventional point-scanning TPM due to emission photon scattering.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 provide quantitative comparison of imaging depths between OT-TP-LSM and 1PLSM in the same skin specimen. The three-fold improvement is clearly demonstrated with specific measurements. The acknowledgment of limitations compared to point-scanning TPM and the explanation of emission photon scattering as the cause shows appropriate critical assessment.

result: OT-TP-LSM successfully visualized 3D cellular structures in human skin cancer specimens, distinguishing between epidermis, dermis, BCC tumor nests, and normal glandular structures (eccrine and sebaceous glands). The 3D visualization capability enabled distinction of normal glands from BCC nests, which could appear similar in 2D images at certain depths.
evaluation: Claims C55-C71 and C142 describe detailed observations from skin cancer specimens with validation by corresponding H&E histology images (C65). The ability to distinguish different tissue structures is demonstrated through multiple ROIs with specific histological features described. The advantage of 3D visualization over 2D imaging (C70-C71) is well-supported by the presented data.

result: In pancreatic specimens, switching from proflavine to propidium iodide (PI) labeling increased imaging depth from approximately 30 μm to 55 μm due to PI's longer emission wavelength (640 nm). OT-TP-LSM successfully visualized normal pancreatic structures (acini, islets of Langerhans, ducts) and premalignant lesions (IPMN and PanIN), with images comparable to H&E histology.
evaluation: Claims C72-C88 demonstrate the methodological optimization for pancreatic tissue and successful imaging of various pancreatic structures. The quantitative improvement in imaging depth with PI is clearly stated with mechanistic explanation. Validation with H&E histology (C86, C88) and citations supporting PI labeling properties (C75, C80) strengthen the findings.

result: OT-TP-LSM visualized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) specimens, showing irregularly shaped cancer glands with disorganized cell arrangement, nuclear membrane distortion, and desmoplastic stroma. The system enabled nondestructive 3D visualization of cancer gland invasiveness that could not be identified from limited 2D information.
evaluation: Claims C89-C97 and C143 describe detailed observations of PDAC with validation by H&E histology. The distinction between nonneoplastic ducts and cancer glands is clearly demonstrated (C94-C96). The diagnostic features described (C92-C93) are supported by citations. The advantage of 3D visualization for detecting invasiveness (C97) is a logical conclusion from the presented data.

result: OT-TP-LSM successfully imaged benign and malignant prostate specimens, distinguishing benign glands with multiple cell layers (secretory and basal cells) from cancer glands with single-layered malignant secretory cells due to loss of basal cell layers. The system provided histological 3D information equivalent to H&E stained images without sectioning.
evaluation: Claims C98-C105 describe prostate imaging with clear distinction between benign and malignant regions validated by H&E histology (C100, C104). The histological features distinguishing benign from malignant glands are well-described (C99, C102-C103). The conclusion about equivalence to H&E histology (C105) is supported by the presented comparisons.

result: PI-labeled OT-TP-LSM images were successfully converted to virtual H&E images using CycleGAN, an unsupervised deep learning network. The virtual H&E images of PanIN and PDAC showed similar patterns to real H&E histology and displayed diagnostic features for discriminating PDAC from PanIN, though some regions were not transformed properly due to insufficient training data.
evaluation: Claims C107-C114, C125, and C162-C173 describe the CycleGAN implementation with appropriate technical details including architecture, training data (14,322 and 22,644 patches), hyperparameters, and hardware specifications. The results show successful style transfer with acknowledged limitations (C109). The diagnostic utility of virtual H&E images (C113) is supported by the presented comparisons.

result: The authors acknowledge that CycleGAN requires further development for robust performance and universal application, with plans to train the network using more OT-TP-LSM images from various tissue types including skin and prostate.
evaluation: Claims C126-C127 appropriately identify limitations of the current CycleGAN implementation and propose specific future work. This is a reasonable assessment given the observed transformation issues (C109) and the limited training to pancreatic specimens.

result: OT-TP-LSM achieved imaging depths of approximately 60 μm in skin, which was sufficient for visualizing 3D cell structures without sectioning artifacts, though imaging depths varied by tissue type and were relatively low in pancreas and prostate compared to skin, possibly due to dense cell composition and higher refractive index.
evaluation: Claims C119-C122 provide tissue-specific imaging depth measurements with appropriate comparison to conventional TPM and mechanistic explanations for observed differences. The assessment that the depth is sufficient for skin imaging (C120) is supported by the demonstrated results. The speculative explanation for lower depths in pancreas and prostate (C122) is reasonable.

result: The authors identify spherical aberration from RI mismatch between the liquid prism and air as a limitation that degraded image resolution, particularly in the imaging arm, and suggest that an immersion objective lens with high NA would improve both resolution and emission light collection efficiency.
evaluation: Claims C128-C130 appropriately identify a technical limitation with clear mechanistic explanation and propose a specific solution. This is consistent with the measured resolution being 128% of theoretical (C49) and demonstrates critical self-assessment.

result: The excitation wavelength of 770 nm was used to efficiently collect intrinsic SHG light, but this limited the imaging depth. The authors suggest that longer excitation wavelengths with long emission wavelength probes would increase imaging depth beyond what was achieved.
evaluation: Claims C133-C134 identify a design trade-off between SHG collection efficiency and imaging depth, with a reasonable suggestion for improvement. This is consistent with the known physics of two-photon excitation and tissue scattering.

result: Despite high-speed imaging, post-processing time was relatively long (loading at ~6.8 s/GB, processing at ~1.7 s/GB) due to large data size (318 GB per cm² per channel), sequential dual-channel processing, and manual stitching. The authors propose FPGA-based acquisition with GPU computing, C++ implementation, and automatic stitching software to address this limitation for intraoperative applications.
evaluation: Claims C135-C139 and C157-C161 provide specific quantitative measurements of processing times and data sizes, identify the bottlenecks, and propose concrete technical solutions. The acknowledgment that this needs resolution for clinical use (C136) is appropriate. The suggestions are technically sound.

result: Human tissue specimens were collected under appropriate IRB approvals (Yonsei University #4-2021-0128 for skin; Asan Medical Center #2021-0393 for pancreas and prostate) following Declaration of Helsinki principles, with deidentified patient information. Specific sample preparation protocols were followed for fresh skin specimens and FFPE tissue blocks.
evaluation: Claims C148-C156 document appropriate ethical approvals, compliance with research standards, and detailed sample preparation protocols. The methods are sufficiently detailed for reproducibility and demonstrate proper research conduct.

result: The authors establish the context and motivation for developing OT-TP-LSM by reviewing limitations of traditional H&E pathology and existing 3D microscopy techniques, including shallow imaging depths of conventional fluorescence microscopy and geometric limitations of conventional TP-LSM for large specimens.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C12-C30 provide appropriate background supported by multiple citations. The limitations of existing methods are well-established in the field. The logical progression from identifying limitations to proposing OT-TP-LSM as a solution is clear and well-supported by cited literature.

result: The authors conclude that OT-TP-LSM enabled nondestructive visualization of detailed 3D cell structures with high contrast, allowed distinction between cancer and normal structures, and detected cancer invasiveness that is challenging with 2D histological images. The high-quality images may be partially attributed to the Bessel beam-based EDOF light sheet, and the system could be useful for rapid and precise nondestructive 3D pathology.
evaluation: Claims C115-C118, C140-C141, and C144 summarize the demonstrated capabilities across multiple tissue types. The conclusions are well-supported by the extensive imaging results presented in skin, pancreas, and prostate specimens. The attribution to Bessel beam technology (C118) is appropriately speculative with citation support.

result: High imaging depths were achieved owing to long excitation wavelengths and long wavelength fluorophores, and 3D visualization of both cells and ECM enhanced cancer detection ability. However, OT-TP-LSM images may be unfamiliar to pathologists accustomed to traditional H&E histology.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 are supported by the demonstrated imaging depths and successful cancer detection across multiple tissue types. The mechanistic explanation (C8) is consistent with known physics. The concern about unfamiliarity (C106) is reasonable and motivates the virtual H&E conversion work.

result: The authors suggest several technical improvements including using an immersion medium with 1.5 RI, applying quick optical clearing methods, and employing multiple Bessel beams for excitation light sheet generation to enhance pixel dwell time and image contrast.
evaluation: Claims C123-C124 and C131 propose improvements with citation support, but these are speculative suggestions for future work without experimental validation in the current study. While the suggestions are technically reasonable and supported by cited literature, they remain untested in the context of OT-TP-LSM.
